reference.title: Forms for records you have seen
reference.shortdesc: The forms on the Add a record sheet that match a census, a register or a certificate, and what each one asks for.

section.title: What the forms are for
section.p: The sheet named has plain forms and forms that match a real record. A plain form, such as , asks for a name and dates. A form that matches a record asks the questions that the record answers. Use it only for a record you have seen, because some of its boxes ask for the record's own words.

Choose at the foot of the sheet to see the rest. The number in brackets says how many there are. A line under a form says when it does not fit. For example, a census form can say that nobody in the tree was alive then.

section.title: The census forms
section.p: There are forms for the censuses of England and Wales, starting with 1841, and one for the 1939 register. A census form says Adding to the household of a person, and you can change whose household it is. The census date is filled in for you.

table.title: What a census form asks for

row.entry: The date, the place, and the title of the source.
The place that keeps the record. Then the class, the piece, the folio and the page, with the schedule number.
The registration district, the sub-district and the enumeration district.
A row for each person in the household. The form lists the family, and leaves out people who had died by the census date.
